intro: Olga Gurevich plays a waltz with three distinct voices: a sighing C♯ minor melody, quick descending quavers and a slower song in D♭ major. The running tune keeps coming back between the others.

sections.label: A · Held notes and small flourishes
sections.mNote: Tempo giusto: a chordal melody above the waltz bass

sections.label: B · Descending quavers
sections.mNote: Più mosso sends the right hand running

sections.label: C · A song in D♭ major
D · Song and returning quavers
sections.mNote: The long melody leads back towards C♯ minor

sections.label: E · The chordal melody again
sections.mNote: Long notes return between the right hand’s flourishes

sections.label: F · The last running refrain
sections.mNote: Descending quavers carry the waltz towards its close

cues.title: Held notes, then a curl
cues.text: Two notes sound together in the right hand and hang across the bar line. A small, quick curl answers them. Below, the left hand keeps leaping from a bass note to two chords. Chopin marks this opening Tempo giusto.
cues.evidence: Score, opening Tempo giusto; engraving by Knute Snortum (2023), p. 1. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/28/IMSLP879636-PMLP2373-waltz-op64-no2.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Quavers take over
cues.text: Più mosso: more movement. The right hand runs down in chains of quavers while the left keeps the bass-and-two-chords pattern. This is the waltz’s recurring tune; it will return after each of the broader melodies.
cues.evidence: Score, first Più mosso, pp. 1–2; its returns appear on pp. 3 and 5. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/28/IMSLP879636-PMLP2373-waltz-op64-no2.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Five flats on the page
cues.text: Four sharps become five flats: D♭ major, the bright twin of C♯ minor on the keyboard. The marking is Più lento, slower. Long melody notes open out above chords that carry their own little answering lines.
cues.evidence: Score, Più lento, pp. 2–3: D♭ major key signature and sustained melody. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/28/IMSLP879636-PMLP2373-waltz-op64-no2.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: After school in Baku
cues.text: As a girl in Baku, Gurevich goes from ordinary school to music school: piano lessons, solfège, music history and choir. At seventeen she moves to Moscow to study at the Gnesin Academy. New York becomes her home in 1998, where she performs and teaches.
cues.evidence: Childhood and Gnesin training: https://www.bsmny.org/team/olga-gurevich-2/. Move to New York: https://www.musiciansclubofny.org/biographies/olgagurevich

cues.title: One last descent
cues.text: The running refrain gets the last word. Its quavers fall, climb back up and fall again; the left hand continues its three-beat tread beneath them. The waltz closes in C♯ minor.
cues.evidence: Score, final Più mosso and C♯ minor cadence, p. 5. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/28/IMSLP879636-PMLP2373-waltz-op64-no2.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He brought the opera singer’s breath and the mazurka’s wayward accents to a piano that could whisper across a room.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; composition with Józef Elsner in Warsaw, 1826–29
Warsaw · Paris from 1831 · summers at Nohant
Piano lessons, publishing and occasional concerts
The piano, from a few lines of mazurka to concertos and sonatas
composer.background:
In February 1832, a twenty-one-year-old Polish pianist played in the Pleyel rooms in Paris. Chopin had arrived the previous autumn, with two concertos behind him. The concert caught the attention of the city’s publishers; teaching soon supplied his living. He would spend the rest of his life in a profession that depended on people hearing him at close quarters. The great public virtuosos travelled from triumph to triumph. Chopin stayed in Paris and gave lessons.

He was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810. His father, Nicolas, had come from France and worked as a tutor; his mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska, was Polish. They moved to Warsaw while Fryderyk was still a baby, when Nicolas obtained a teaching post at the Lyceum. At seven the boy already had a polonaise in print. Wojciech Żywny taught him the piano, with Bach and Mozart among his models; Józef Elsner later gave him a rigorous training in composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music.
